lead: A signal leaves the transmitter clean, but the medium does not preserve it. It gets weaker (attenuation), its shape smears (distortion), and unwanted energy joins it (noise). These three impairments decide how far a link can run, what bandwidth it can carry and how many errors the receiver sees. Only a few universities teach transmission impairments as a chapter of their own. The ideas appear inside every physical-layer design, from a broadband cable in Chennai to a fibre link between cell towers.
prereq: You need 2.1 for signal power, frequency and the sine wave.

blocks.text: Attenuation is loss of signal power along the medium. A long cable, a poor connector or a high-resistance conductor turns some signal energy into heat. The receiver sees a smaller wave, so it is harder to detect against noise. Attenuation is measured in decibels (dB), a logarithmic unit that turns multiplication of losses into addition.

blocks.where: P₁ and P₂ are input and output powers in the same unit; dB is the change.
V₁ and V₂ are input and output voltages; use 20 log₁₀ only for voltage or current ratios.

blocks.text: A negative dB value means loss: −3 dB halves power. A positive value is gain. dBm is power relative to 1 mW: P(dBm) = 10 log₁₀(P/1 mW). In a cable, loss grows with distance and with frequency, so a long high-frequency link needs repeaters or amplifiers. Engineers add dB along a link: cable loss plus connector loss plus splitter loss. For example, 10 km at 3 dB/km gives 30 dB loss, a factor of 1000.

sections.h3: Distortion and noise: shape and unwanted energy

blocks.text: Distortion changes the shape of a signal. In a composite signal, different frequency components travel at slightly different speeds in the medium. They arrive out of step, so the sum at the receiver is not a scaled copy of the sum at the sender.

The smearing makes adjacent bits overlap. This overlap is intersymbol interference (ISI). An equaliser is a filter that compensates for the delay differences; filter design belongs to a signals course. Overmodulation in an analog transmitter also clips peaks, but that is a sender fault, not a medium impairment.
Noise is unwanted energy that joins the signal. Thermal noise comes from random electron motion in any resistor.

blocks.where: vₙ² is mean-square noise voltage; Pₙ is available noise power; k is Boltzmann constant (1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K); T is absolute temperature in kelvin; B is bandwidth in Hz; R is resistance in ohms.

items: Induced noise enters from nearby wires or motors.
Crosstalk is coupling from a neighbouring signal pair.
Impulse noise is a short spike from switching or lightning.

blocks.text: Signal-to-noise ratio compares signal power S to noise power N. Use the same unit for both. SNRdB = 10 log₁₀(S/N). A ratio of 100 is 20 dB. Higher SNR means easier detection; Shannon capacity uses it directly.

figure.caption: Each kilometre of cable costs 3 dB, so the 10 mW (10 dBm) signal drops in a straight line to 0.316 mW (−5 dBm) at 5 km, while the noise floor stays flat at 0.020 mW (−17 dBm). At 5 km the vertical gap between the two lines is exactly the 12.0 dB SNR of the worked example.

spec.aria: A straight line falls from 10 dBm at 0 km to minus 5 dBm at 5 km, losing 3 dB every kilometre, while a flat line at minus 17 dBm marks the noise floor; at 5 km the gap between the lines is 12 dB, the signal-to-noise ratio.

examples.question: A 10 mW signal enters a 5 km cable whose loss is 3 dB per km. Find the output power. The noise at the output is 20 µW; find the signal-to-noise ratio in dB.
examples.answer: Output power is 0.316 mW, S/N is 15.8, and SNR is about 12.0 dB.
examples.check:
import math
P_in_mW = 10.0
loss_per_km_dB = 3.0
distance_km = 5.0
noise_mW = 20e-3
total_loss_dB = loss_per_km_dB * distance_km
P_out_mW = P_in_mW * 10 ** (-total_loss_dB / 10)
snr_ratio = P_out_mW / noise_mW
snr_dB = 10 * math.log10(snr_ratio)
print(round(P_out_mW, 3))
print(round(snr_ratio, 1))
print(round(snr_dB, 1))

traps: Using 10 log₁₀ for a voltage ratio. Voltage and current ratios use 20 log₁₀; power ratios use 10 log₁₀.
Dropping the minus sign and reporting a loss as a gain. −3 dB is a loss; +3 dB is a gain.
Confusing dB with dBm. dB is a ratio; dBm is an absolute power relative to 1 mW.
Forgetting to put signal and noise in the same unit before computing S/N.
Confusing attenuation with distortion. Attenuation changes height; distortion changes shape.

quiz.q: Why does a composite signal suffer distortion while a pure sine wave does not change shape?
quiz.a: A composite signal has several frequencies. They travel at different speeds and arrive out of step, so the sum changes shape. A pure sine has one frequency.

quiz.q: A cable has 6 dB loss. Input is 4 mW. Find output power.
A voltage falls from 2 V to 1 V. Find the dB change.
quiz.a: 20 log₁₀(1/2) = 20 × (−0.301) = −6.02 dB, a loss of about 6 dB.

quiz.q: Why does thermal noise power rise with bandwidth?
quiz.a: Pₙ = kTB. Wider B admits more frequency components, so more random noise power.

quiz.q: A receiver has S/N = 1000. Find SNR<sub>dB</sub> and say what it means.
quiz.a: SNR<sub>dB</sub> = 10 log₁₀(1000) = 30 dB. Signal power is 1000 times noise power, so detection is easier.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, link budgets add every dB of loss and every noise source before choosing an amplifier or repeater. Fibre and DSL engineers measure attenuation against frequency, not just distance, because high frequencies fade faster. 5G and Wi-Fi planners use SNR to pick modulation and coding.
